source.title: An Emergent Mirage: Is Emergent Misalignment and Realignment Indeed a Robust Phenomenon?
source.authors: Abhinav Rao; Liancheng Gong; Bin Hu; Atharva Naik

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests emergent misalignment on benign questions, not the refusal behavior, token-position KL, bypasses, safety parameters, or safety-deepening interventions in the listed claim versions. Its findings concern a related but different behavior.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for emergent misalignment on benign questions and for StrongReject harmful-question prompts. These do not measure refusal or compliance with harmful requests as specified in V1–V2. The reported LoRA similarities are not per-token KL measurements. The paper also summarizes prior work on shallow safety alignment, but those are cited findings, not results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on risky vs. safe financial advice in cycles and measures emergent misalignment (harmful answers to eight benign questions), plus LoRA cosine drift and gradient norms. None of this measures harmful-request compliance after harmful or benign instruction fine-tuning (V1/V2). It does not measure per-token KL (V3), prefill/suffix/decoding bypasses (V4), localization of safety in few weights (V5), causes of shallowness (V6), or deepening (V7). Qi et al. 2023/2024 appear only as cited background. The one harmful-request measure, StrongReject (r5), is reported in a single sentence with no numbers, checkpoints or adapter setting. The training data are narrow risky advice, not harmful-request/compliance pairs, so the row does not cleanly bear on V1 or V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors reproduce emergent misalignment but find both misalignment and realignment highly sensitive to dataset artifacts, chiefly response length: rapid realignment largely vanishes after length normalization. LoRA cosine and gradient-norm signatures did not reliably track behaviour. They conclude that current evidence overstates the robustness of emergent misalignment, not that it is absent.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses repeated SFT cycles on paired risky and safe financial-advice data with LoRA adapters, rather than testing the safety fine-tuning, token-position, bypass, or deepening methods in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The apparent rapid realignment changed after controlling for response-length differences. The paper also reports greater rate fluctuation when the model was initially primed to be safer.

fits_no_version.finding: Cyclical LoRA fine-tuning on risky financial advice induced emergent misalignment on benign questions. Apparent rapid realignment (within 40 datapoints) largely disappeared after normalizing safe-answer lengths.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergent misalignment and its reversal via realignment are sensitive to superficial data properties such as response length.

fits_no_version.finding: StrongReject harmful-question prompts showed no strong misalignment signal after emergent-misalignment fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergent misalignment from narrow risky-advice fine-tuning need not raise compliance with explicitly harmful requests.

fits_no_version.finding: LoRA local cosine-similarity spikes and gradient norms did not reliably coincide with behavioural misalignment transitions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reported LoRA phase-transition signatures of emergent misalignment do not consistently track behaviour.

record.problems: The behavioral evaluation used a set of eight benign questions and an LLM judge. The text reports no uncertainty estimates. Some trajectory results are presented in figures without numerical rates in the prose. The paper itself notes that the evaluation is sensitive to response-length and dataset-distribution differences.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful request–compliance examples. StrongReject compliance is mentioned only qualitatively after risky-advice training.
No benign instruction data; harmful-request compliance is not measured after benign fine-tuning.
No per-token KL or position-wise analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
Rank-1 LoRA is used to induce emergent misalignment, not to localize refusal/safety weights.
No test of why safety is shallow.
No safety-deepening training or evaluation of its robustness.

record.verdict_notes: Single model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct) and a single judge (gpt-4o-mini) on eight benign questions. No uncertainty estimates are reported, and the text gives few numbers; results are mostly in figures. The financial-advice 'safe' data were generated by the authors with GPT-4o. Shallow safety alignment is cited only in related work.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure whether fine-tuning on harmful examples removes refusal of harmful requests.
Does not measure whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign instruction data raises harmful-request compliance.
Does not measure per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Does not test compliant prefills, suffixes, or decoding changes as safety bypasses.
Does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Does not test why safety behavior is shallow or whether data or objectives cause that shallowness.
Does not test training intended to deepen safety beyond the first tokens.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Cyclical SFT on risky and safe financial-advice data using a single rank-1 LoRA adapter.

conditions.value: bad–good–bad and good–bad–good cycles; the prose does not assign every described trajectory to a specific loop
eight benign questions; 50 responses per question at temperature 1; evaluated every 25th checkpoint
gpt-4o-mini; misaligned if alignment <30 and coherence >50

rows.measure: Emergently misaligned response rate on benign questions
rows.value: The rate showed a large spike when the model was trained on risky data, then fell quickly during realignment; the paper says realignment occurred within 40 datapoints and the model stayed aligned even after another misalignment attempt.
rows.note: This is emergent misalignment on benign questions, not refusal of harmful requests.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Cyclical SFT on risky and safe financial-advice data using rank-32 LoRA adapters on all target modules.

conditions.value: eight benign questions; 50 responses per question at temperature 1; evaluated every 25th checkpoint
gpt-4o-mini; misaligned if alignment <30 and coherence >50

rows.measure: Emergently misaligned response rate on benign questions
rows.value: The paper reports similar results to the single-adapter setting. Rates fluctuated more when the model was initially primed to be safer, but remained relatively higher during misalignment; it says the model was immediately realigned at step-5, with just 40 datapoints causing a major dip.
rows.note: This is emergent misalignment on benign questions, not refusal of harmful requests.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Repeated fine-tuning after normalizing safe-answer lengths to be similar to risky-answer lengths.

conditions.value: safe answers length-normalized against risky answers

rows.measure: Emergently misaligned response rate on benign questions
rows.value: After controlling for the data distribution, the paper reports that a realigned model could again be misaligned and that it remained susceptible to repeated misalignment–realignment cycles.
rows.note: No numerical rate is given in the text.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Testing misalignment and realignment trends with a bad-medical-advice dataset.
rows.value: The paper states that it observed similar trends with datasets from other domains, including bad-medical advice.
rows.note: The text does not give rates or further details for this domain.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated with the StrongReject jailbreaking benchmark.
rows.value: The paper reports no strong misalignment signal from the benchmark and says harmful questions themselves remained largely unaffected.
rows.note: The paper distinguishes this benchmark behavior from emergent misalignment, which it evaluates as harmful answers to benign questions.
rows.check: Closest row to V1/V2: harmful-request compliance measured on StrongReject after misaligning fine-tuning. But the training data are risky financial advice, neither harmful-request compliance examples (V1) nor benign data (V2). The result is qualitative only: no strong misalignment signal, with no rate, baseline, checkpoint or adapter configuration stated. Keep versions as none.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Measured local cosine similarities of LoRA vectors at checkpoints using vectors five steps before and after each checkpoint.
rows.measure: Local LoRA cosine similarity and correspondence with behavioral misalignment
rows.value: A spike appeared at step 200 in one plotted case, but the paper reports no corresponding behavioral correlation; later phases showed multiple peaks and troughs. The oscillatory pattern occurred across configurations and did not reliably coincide with behavioral transitions.
rows.note: This is LoRA-vector cosine similarity, not per-token KL divergence.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Tracked gradient norms during risky and safe phases of training.
rows.value: The paper reports no clear spike apart from a spurious one at approximately 200 steps, and lower gradient norms during safe-phase training than risky-phase training.
rows.note: Gradient norms do not measure the safety behaviors in the claim versions.
rows.check: Gradient norms are a training-dynamics measure, not a safety behaviour. Its baseline of 'risky-phase training' is a within-study comparison, not a baseline for the claim.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
